strengths: The core idea is conceptually elegant and practical: associating attention heads with reference frames from Platonic solid symmetry groups and applying RoPE per frame allows incorporating discrete roto-reflection and continuous translation equivariance without changing standard Transformer tensor shapes or computational graphs.

The paper provides an insightful theoretical connection between linear RoPE attention and dynamic content-aware convolution (Proposition 2), offering a principled derivation and a practical linear-time O(N) formulation for 3D point cloud modeling.

By keeping the total feature dimension C x |G| constant, the architecture runs at speeds comparable to standard PyTorch Transformer layers, overcoming the severe computational overhead of continuous steerable tensor-product methods (demonstrated in wall-clock benchmarks in Table 4).
The Fourier domain formulation of the group linear layers (Appendix M) is theoretically rigorous and demonstrates concrete throughput gains at larger hidden dimensions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple modalities: 2D vision (CIFAR-10), 3D point clouds (ScanObjectNN), and molecular property prediction on both standard (QM9) and large-scale (OMol25) benchmarks.
weaknesses: Equivariance is restricted to discrete subgroups of O(3) (e.g., tetrahedral or octahedral symmetries) rather than continuous SO(3)/E(3), which can still exhibit orientation sensitivity under arbitrary continuous rotations unless augmented with PCA frames or data augmentation.

On OMol25 (Table 5), the comparison with literature state-of-the-art is conducted under a restricted 120-hour compute budget where the model outperforms the compute-matched eSEN baseline, but results are not yet reported for fully converged training matching the literature compute budget (~475 GPU-hours).

Absolute classification performance on ScanObjectNN (81.3% - 82.0%) is modest compared to specialized state-of-the-art 3D point cloud backbones; although the controlled comparison against the baseline transformer (80.5%) clearly validates the effect of the geometric inductive bias, contextualizing with domain SOTA would be beneficial.

strengths: Principled and elegant unification of Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) and discrete subgroup equivariance: The paper shows that by projecting relative coordinates or steering RoPE base frequencies across Platonic solid symmetry frames, one can construct an E(n)/SE(n)-equivariant transformer without altering standard transformer computation graphs or incurring asymptotic overhead.

Insightful connection to dynamic convolution: Proposition 2 and Section 4 establish that RoPE linear attention with constant keys is mathematically equivalent to dynamic convolution parameterized via sparse Fourier coefficients, naturally enabling an O(N) linear-complexity formulation.

Strong efficiency and wall-clock inference speed: Unlike traditional Clebsch-Gordan or steerable kernel architectures (e.g., TFN), the Platonic Transformer runs at the same speed as a standard TransformerEncoderLayer, outperforming prior equivariant baselines by multiple orders of magnitude in inference latency.
Thorough mathematical exposition and Appendix work: The Fourier domain implementation on finite groups (Appendix M) and the formal proofs in Appendices A–E are well-developed and clear.
weaknesses: Unfinished Related Works section: Appendix B consists solely of placeholder bullet lists with bare citations (e.g., 'Equivariant Transformers. SE(3) Transformer, EFA, G-Hyena, EScAIP, GATr') without any accompanying explanatory text or discussion.

Limited evaluation on standard benchmarks: On QM9 (Table 3), the authors evaluate on only 2 out of the 12 standard chemical properties (dipole moment $\mu$ and isotropic polarizability $\alpha$). Standard practice in the geometric deep learning literature requires reporting the full 12 targets.

Lack of continuous equivariance error quantification: Because the Platonic groups discretize SO(3) into 12 or 24 rotations, the model is only strictly equivariant to discrete subgroups and approximately equivariant to continuous SO(3). The paper does not evaluate or quantify the continuous rotation error / equivariance deviation under arbitrary continuous rotations.

Performance ceilings on point cloud and large-scale molecular benchmarks: On ScanObjectNN (PB_T50_RS), overall accuracy is around 81–82%, whereas dedicated point cloud transformers routinely achieve 88–90%+. On OMol25, while the model is competitive under a 120-hour compute budget, it falls notably short of fully converged literature baselines (e.g., eSEN MAE of 10.11 vs. 24.25 for forces).

strengths: Principled and elegant conceptual framework: Lifting standard Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) across reference frames of discrete Platonic subgroups (e.g., tetrahedral, octahedral) to achieve roto-translation equivariance within unmodified Transformer architectures.

Preservation of standard Transformer computational structure: By aligning group elements with attention heads and structuring linear layers as discrete group convolutions (or block-diagonal operations in the group Fourier domain), the architecture maintains standard matrix-multiplication operations and hardware-friendly execution.

Theoretical connection to dynamic convolution: Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 provide insightful framing by showing that linear RoPE attention with constant keys acts as a content-adaptive geometric convolution in the Fourier basis, running in linear time O(N).

Solid throughput and speed advantages: Inference benchmarks (Table 4) demonstrate speeds matching vanilla Transformers and outperforming tensor-product / spherical harmonic-based equivariant networks (such as TFN) by orders of magnitude.
weaknesses: Incomplete evaluation on standard benchmarks: On QM9 (Table 3), the evaluation is restricted to only two targets (dipole moment $\mu$ and isotropic polarizability $\alpha$) out of the standard 12 quantum chemical properties. Reporting across all 12 properties is standard protocol in the geometric deep learning literature.

Discrete vs. continuous equivariance trade-off: The method achieves exact equivariance only with respect to discrete subgroups (e.g., 12 rotations for tetrahedral, 24 for octahedral), meaning continuous SO(3) equivariance is only approximate. The paper does not systematically quantify the residual error under arbitrary out-of-group continuous rotations.

Under-converged comparison on OMol25: While compute-matched benchmarking against eSEN on OMol25 (Table 5) at 120 GPU-hours is appreciated, the model remains far from fully converged literature baselines (e.g., eSEN force MAE 10.11 vs. 24.25 reported here), leaving asymptotic scaling potential partially unverified.

Restrictions of the linear convolutional variant: The linear-time dynamic convolution formulation relies on fixing key vectors ($k_j = 1$) to avoid training instability observed with mixed kernels on QM9/OMol25, which comes at the expense of empirical performance compared to full softmax attention.

strengths: Elegantly bridges group equivariance and standard Transformer architectures: By pairing Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) with reference frames defined by Platonic solid symmetry groups, the model achieves discrete roto-reflection and continuous translation equivariance without modifying the standard Transformer computation graph or incurring overhead in standard attention kernels (e.g., FlashAttention).

Solid theoretical analysis connecting RoPE-attention and dynamic group convolutions: Proposition 4.1 and Section 4 rigorously show that linear RoPE attention acts as an adaptive content-aware convolution in a sparse Fourier basis, directly enabling an $O(N)$ linear-time variant for long sequences.

Comprehensive and multi-domain empirical evaluation: The paper demonstrates consistent benefits across both non-equivariant benchmarks (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, ScanObjectNN) and physically symmetric tasks (QM9 molecule generation and regression, OMol25 interatomic potentials, ProteinMD).

Strong practical scalability results: On OMol25 4M, the model significantly outperforms eSEN-sm across force and energy MAE while running with a 2.6x higher training throughput. Similarly, the linear variant achieves state-of-the-art results on ProteinMD.

Thorough ablations and extensions: The paper includes thoughtful studies on key design choices, including fixed vs. learned keys (and optimization stability), invariant vs. equivariant attention scores, and a group Fourier domain formulation (Appendix O) that reduces FLOPs.
weaknesses: Approximate rather than continuous rotational equivariance: Equivariance is exact only with respect to discrete finite subgroups (e.g., tetrahedral or octahedral), while continuous $SO(3)$ equivariance is only approximate. While the authors evaluate equivariance error in Appendix N.1, certain physical systems with strict conservation laws (e.g., angular momentum) may still demand exact continuous equivariance.

Performance gap of the linear convolutional variant: On computer vision and point cloud tasks (Tables 1 and 2), the linear-time dynamic convolution counterpart suffers a noticeable performance penalty (around 5–6 percentage points) compared to softmax attention, indicating that the kernel expansion without softmax struggles with complex localized semantic interactions.

Limited baseline comparisons on OMol25: While the comparison to eSEN-sm in Table 5 is favorable and well-controlled in terms of throughput, broader comparisons against other recent large-scale MLIP architectures (or clearer positioning within the OMol25 benchmark leaderboard) would further validate its standing.

Specialized models remain stronger on specific QM9 targets: As shown in Table 10, specialized equivariant architectures (e.g., PaiNN, SphereNet, EquiformerV2) still outperform Platonic Transformer on several thermochemical targets, indicating that a general geometric prior does not yet fully replace task-specific geometric graph inductive biases.

strengths: Principled and practical architectural formulation: The paper integrates discrete subgroup roto-reflection equivariance and continuous translation equivariance into standard Transformers via RoPE frame-steering and weight-sharing across heads without modifying the standard computation graph.

Insightful theoretical link to dynamic convolution: Proposition 4.1 clearly derives how unnormalized RoPE attention acts as a dynamic content-aware convolution in the sparse Fourier basis, naturally enabling a linear-time convolutional mode with O(N) complexity.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: The method is validated across non-equivariant 2D/3D tasks (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, ScanObjectNN) and equivariant scientific benchmarks (QM9 property prediction & generation, OMol25 interatomic potential, and ProteinMD), consistently demonstrating competitive accuracy and superior runtime efficiency compared to heavy continuous equivariant architectures.

Thorough appendix and ablation studies: The submission includes detailed analyses of optimization stability (learned vs. fixed keys), equivariance error across training, wall-clock timing breakdowns on modern hardware (H100/H200), and a Fourier domain implementation for accelerating group linear layers.
weaknesses: Equivariance is restricted to discrete subgroups: Unlike steerable GNNs or Clebsch-Gordan-based architectures that guarantee continuous SO(3)/E(3) equivariance, the Platonic Transformer only provides exact equivariance to discrete finite groups (e.g., tetrahedral or octahedral), relying on data augmentation or test-time averaging for continuous rotations.

Sensitivity to key parametrization across task scales: The attention mechanism requires noticeably different design choices across datasets (e.g., fixed keys kj=1 are necessary to prevent divergence on QM9, whereas learned keys with QK-normalization are required for OMol25), suggesting that practitioners must carefully calibrate expressivity versus stability depending on dataset size and modality.

Performance trade-offs on specialized molecular targets: On some standard QM9 thermochemical and spatial targets (e.g., U, U0, R^2), established target-specialized architectures (such as PaiNN, TorchMD-NET, or SphereNet) still outperform the proposed architecture, indicating that the general geometric bias does not entirely substitute for specialized physical priors.

strengths: Principled and scalable formulation: The paper proposes an elegant way to incorporate discrete roto-reflection equivariance (subgroups of O(n) such as Platonic solid symmetry groups) into standard Transformers by coupling RoPE with group reference frames and group-equivariant linear layers. This retains the standard Transformer computational graph and throughput while achieving exact discrete and approximate continuous equivariance.

Theoretical connection to dynamic convolution: Proposition 4.1 and Corollary 4.3 provide an insightful link between linear RoPE-based attention and dynamic content-adaptive convolutions in a sparse Fourier basis, offering a clear mathematical foundation and an efficient O(N) linear-complexity formulation.

Broad and varied empirical validation: The framework is evaluated across diverse settings, ranging from non-equivariant 2D/3D perception tasks (CIFAR-10, ImageNet-1K, ScanObjectNN) to equivariant scientific benchmarks (QM9 molecule generation and property prediction, ProteinMD dynamics, and large-scale OMol25 4M).

Strong computational efficiency: Wall-clock profiling demonstrates that Platonic Transformers match the inference and training throughput of standard Transformers, overcoming the severe runtime and scaling bottlenecks typically associated with Clebsch-Gordan tensor product-based equivariant models (e.g., TFN, G-Hyena). Furthermore, the Fourier-domain linear layer formulation in Appendix O highlights concrete pathways for additional speedups at wider channels.
weaknesses: Subgroup approximation rather than continuous equivariance: Because the method enforces equivariance only over discrete finite subgroups (e.g., tetrahedral or octahedral groups), continuous SO(3)/SE(3) transformations still incur non-zero equivariance errors (as quantified in Table 13), requiring rotational data augmentation or test-time averaging to mitigate residual orientation variance.

Sub-optimal performance on fine-grained physical targets: On QM9 molecular property regression (Table 10), while Platonic Transformer outperforms the trivial translation-only baseline, it remains behind specialized continuous equivariant architectures (such as EquiformerV2, PaiNN, and TorchMD-NET) on several key thermochemical and energy targets (U, U0, H, G).

Optimization sensitivity and reliance on fixed keys: As discussed in Section 4.1 and Appendix M, utilizing learned key projections (kj = WK fj) leads to severe optimization instability/divergence on smaller physical datasets like QM9 unless constrained by heavy regularization or QK normalization. Relying on constant keys (kj = 1) avoids this but strips away pairwise key-query feature matching, reducing the attention mechanism purely to content-adaptive spatial filtering.
